content: Mode selection: This rewrite decision is multidimensional and requires at least three incommensurable lenses. (1) CAUSAL — will switching to Rust mechanistically produce the safety and performance outcomes we desire, or do the real failure modes lie elsewhere (logic bugs, config, architecture)? (2) BAYESIAN — given our team's current Rust proficiency and the migration scope, what is the posterior probability of an on-time, regression-free delivery? (3) ENGINEERING/CONSTRAINT — what are the hard constraints that any solution must satisfy regardless of language choice: zero-downtime migration, backward-compatible JWT handling, budget ceiling, rollback safety? Selecting primaryMode=sequential to structure the overall decision chain; secondary lenses (causal, bayesian, engineering) are applied in thoughts 2–4 before converging in thought 5.
assumptions: The team has partial but not majority Rust production experience (≤3 of ~10 engineers)
The current auth system has documented incident history distinguishing language-layer from logic-layer bugs
Migration must be zero-downtime with no forced client re-authentication
There is a meaningful budget and timeline ceiling (not an open-ended R&D project)
switchReason: Safety, performance, team expertise, and migration cost are four structurally different concerns: causal mechanisms, probabilistic risk, and hard engineering constraints cannot be collapsed into a single mode without losing critical information.

content: CAUSAL lens — Mechanisms and failure attribution: The core causal question is whether the current auth system's failure modes are language-layer (memory unsafety: buffer overflows, use-after-free, data races) or logic-layer (misconfigured token expiry windows, RBAC policy bugs, timing-attack vulnerabilities in comparison functions, session fixation). Rust eliminates the former class entirely and provides excellent tooling for the latter (type-state patterns can enforce valid token states at compile time). However, empirical data on auth system incidents across the industry suggests ~70–80% of auth security failures are logic bugs, not memory-safety bugs — especially in managed-language implementations (Java, Go, Node) that already prevent the memory-safety class. If the current system is written in a memory-safe language, the causal benefit of Rust is significantly narrower than it first appears. Performance is a more genuine causal win: Rust's zero-cost abstractions and absence of GC pauses can materially reduce tail latency and throughput — but only if auth is currently a measured bottleneck. If auth latency is not on the critical path, the performance gain is real but irrelevant to system outcomes. Causal conclusion: Rust solves a real but potentially small subset of the failure modes; the benefit is strongest if (a) the current language is unsafe (C/C++) or (b) auth is a measured throughput bottleneck.
assumptions: Current auth system is written in a memory-managed language (not C/C++)
Incident post-mortems exist and have been classified by failure class
Auth service performance has been profiled; any bottleneck data is available

content: BAYESIAN lens — Probability of success given team expertise: Let H = 'rewrite ships on time with zero regressions.' We estimate the prior across comparable rewrite projects at P(H) ≈ 0.40 (full rewrites of security-critical systems are notoriously high-risk; new-language rewrites add a significant multiplier). Updating on evidence: (A) If ≤3/10 engineers have production Rust experience, the team will spend significant time learning borrow-checker patterns, async Rust idioms, and ecosystem tooling (tokio, tower, axum) — this increases schedule variance and regression probability; posterior shifts toward P(H) ≈ 0.30–0.35. (B) If the auth system is small (<5k LOC, few external integrations) the risk is lower; P(H) rises toward 0.50. (C) If there is no prior experience writing security-critical cryptographic code in Rust (e.g., safe use of ring, RustCrypto), subtle misuse risk is elevated — Rust memory safety does NOT protect against API misuse (e.g., nonce reuse in AEAD). Bayesian conclusion: For a team with limited Rust expertise rewriting a security-critical system with a fixed deadline, the posterior probability of a successful first-attempt delivery is approximately 0.30–0.40, which is below a typical 0.65–0.70 threshold for proceeding without a staged strategy. This does not mean 'never,' but it strongly argues for an incremental or skills-first approach.
assumptions: Team Rust production experience: 2–3 engineers of ~10
No existing Rust codebase in the monorepo to reuse
Deadline is fixed (not open-ended)
Security review/audit is required before shipping

content: ENGINEERING/CONSTRAINT lens — Migration cost and hard constraints: Three hard constraints bound the solution space regardless of language choice. (1) ZERO-DOWNTIME: Auth systems cannot be taken offline; any migration must run old and new systems in parallel with traffic shadowing and graduated rollout. This constraint is language-agnostic but multiplies implementation effort: the team must build a parallel-run harness, divergence detection, and a dual-write/dual-validate period. Estimated overhead: 4–8 additional engineering-weeks. (2) BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: Existing JWTs, session tokens, and API keys must remain valid during transition. This requires the new system to replicate the exact token generation/validation logic of the old system before the old system is decommissioned — a correctness burden that scales with the complexity of the existing token schema. (3) ROLLBACK SAFETY: If the new system produces incorrect auth decisions (false denies or false permits), rollback must be instantaneous. This requires feature-flag infrastructure and the ability to route 100% traffic back to the old system within seconds. Migration cost estimate: A Rust rewrite of a moderate auth system (5–15k LOC) with these three hard constraints in place is realistically a 4–6 month project for a team with adequate Rust expertise; with limited expertise, 7–10 months is more likely. This compares to 6–10 weeks for targeted hardening of logic bugs in the current language. Engineering conclusion: The constraints are surmountable but they double or triple the expected cost relative to naive rewrite estimates.
assumptions: No existing parallel-run or traffic-shadowing infrastructure
JWT schema is moderately complex (custom claims, refresh token rotation)
Feature-flag system exists or can be stood up quickly
Auth system is 5–15k LOC with 3–5 external dependencies (DB, cache, secrets manager)

content: CONVERGENCE: Integrating all three lenses into a recommendation. CAUSAL verdict: Rust would materially improve safety only if the current language is unsafe (C/C++) or auth is a proven throughput bottleneck; for managed-language systems, the causal benefit is real but narrower than advertised — logic bugs dominate failure modes regardless of language. BAYESIAN verdict: With limited team Rust expertise, the posterior probability of on-time, regression-free delivery (P ≈ 0.30–0.40) is below the threshold for a high-stakes security system. ENGINEERING verdict: Zero-downtime, backward-compat, and rollback constraints multiply the true migration cost to 7–10 months, versus 6–10 weeks for hardening the existing system. RECOMMENDATION: Do NOT rewrite the auth system in Rust now. Instead, pursue a three-phase strategy: (Phase 1, now–Q3) Fix the dominant logic-layer vulnerabilities in the current language — this addresses ~70–80% of actual failure modes at low cost and risk. (Phase 2, Q3–Q4) Build Rust expertise deliberately: write a new non-critical internal service in Rust to give 5+ engineers production experience. (Phase 3, Q1 next year) Reassess: if auth is now a measured bottleneck or the team's Rust fluency is strong, a scoped Rust rewrite (starting with the token-validation hot path, not the full system) becomes viable with a much higher probability of success. This phased approach reduces risk, accelerates the fix for real failure modes, and builds the expertise required for any future Rust investment to succeed.
assumptions: Current auth system is in a memory-managed language
Team Rust expertise: 2–3 of ~10 engineers
Logic-layer bugs are the dominant incident class (based on incident history)
A non-critical Rust greenfield service can be staffed in parallel
Timeline is not an emergency — there is no active breach forcing an immediate rewrite
